title: Das Dietmarsische Lügenmärchen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 159. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved (gieng, saß).
about: KHM 159 is a companion piece to 158: another cascade of impossibilities — roasted chickens flying belly-up toward heaven, a deaf man who spots a hare, a blind man who catches it, ships that sail clean over a mountain and drown — told in the spirit of a boasting-match in lies. Despite its title naming Dithmarschen, the region on the North Sea coast, the printed text here is ordinary High German, not the Low German of that place; no dialect is at play.

sentences.n: The tale opens by addressing its hearers directly — “euch,” the old respectful plural — and it will close the same way. Dithmarschen is a marsh district on the North Sea coast of Holstein; despite the setting, the 1857 printing gives this tale in High German, not in the Low German of the region.

sentences.t: Ich sah zwei gebratene Hühner fliegen, flogen schnell und hatten die Bäuche gen Himmel gekehrt, die Rücken nach der Hölle,
sentences.l: I saw two roasted hens flying, flew fast and had their bellies turned toward heaven, their backs toward hell,
sentences.i: I saw two roast hens flying — flying fast, with their bellies turned toward heaven and their backs toward hell,
sentences.n: “gekehrt” is kehren in its sense ‘to turn,’ not ‘to sweep.’ “gen” is the archaic preposition for gegen, ‘toward.’ A roast hen is dead and plucked; the lie is laid on in layers, and the position of the bellies is reported as though it were the point.

sentences.t: und ein Amboß und ein Mühlstein schwammen über den Rhein, fein langsam und leise,
sentences.l: and an anvil and a millstone swam across the Rhine, nice and slowly and quietly,
sentences.n: “fein” here is not ‘fine, delicate’ but the spoken intensifier before an adverb — ‘nice and slowly.’ “Amboß” is the 1857 spelling of Amboss; anvil and millstone are both proverbially the heaviest things there are.

sentences.t: und ein Frosch saß und fraß eine Pflugschaar zu Pfingsten auf dem Eis.
sentences.l: and a frog sat and ate a ploughshare at Whitsun on the ice.
sentences.n: Three impossibilities in the one clause: a frog cannot eat iron, “Pflugschaar” (1857 for Pflugschar) is the iron blade of a plough, and Whitsun falls in late spring, when there is no ice. “fraß” is fressen, the verb used of animals eating.

sentences.t: Da waren drei Kerle, wollten einen Hasen fangen, giengen auf Krücken und Stelzen,
sentences.l: There were three fellows, wanted to catch a hare, went on crutches and stilts,
sentences.i: There were three fellows who meant to catch a hare, and they went on crutches and stilts,
sentences.n: The text says three and then names four — deaf, blind, dumb, and one who could not stir a foot. That is what the 1857 printing does, and it is not corrected here; in a lying-tale a count that will not add up is simply one lie more.

sentences.t: der eine war taub, der zweite blind, der dritte stumm, und der vierte konnte keinen Fuß rühren.
sentences.l: the one was deaf, the second blind, the third dumb, and the fourth could not stir a foot.
sentences.i: the first was deaf, the second blind, the third dumb, and the fourth could not stir a foot.
sentences.n: German begins such a list with “der eine,” ‘the one,’ where English says ‘the first.’ “rühren” here is simply to stir or move, not anrühren ‘to touch.’

sentences.t: Wollt ihr wissen, wie das geschah?
sentences.l: Do you want to know how that happened?
sentences.i: Would you like to know how that came about?
sentences.n: “Wollt ihr” is the old plural address again, turned on the listener at precisely the point where the story stops holding together.

sentences.t: Der Blinde der sah zuerst den Hasen über Feld traben,
sentences.l: The blind one he saw first the hare trotting across field,
sentences.i: The blind one was the first to see the hare trotting across the field,
sentences.n: “Der Blinde” is the adjective blind used as a noun, ‘the blind man’; the tale does the same with “der Stumme” and “der Lahme.” The resumptive “der” after the subject is the spoken syntax this tale runs on throughout. “über Feld” without an article is the old adverbial phrase, ‘over open country.’

sentences.t: der Stumme der rief dem Lahmen zu, und der Lahme faßte ihn beim Kragen.
sentences.l: the dumb one he called out to the lame one, and the lame one seized it by the collar.
sentences.i: the dumb one called out to the lame one, and the lame one caught it by the scruff.
sentences.n: “rief … zu” is zurufen, to call out to someone, with the particle at the end. “der Lahme” is the lame man; this tale is High German throughout, so the word carries no dialect. Each of the three who act does exactly what his affliction forbids; the deaf man is named at the outset and then never appears again.

sentences.t: Etliche die wollten zu Land segeln und spannten die Segel im Wind und schifften über große Äcker hin:
sentences.l: Some, they wanted to sail by land and spread the sails in the wind and shipped away across great ploughed fields:
sentences.i: Some meant to sail overland, and they spread their sails to the wind and went shipping off across great ploughed fields:
sentences.n: “zu Land” is by land, the opposite of zu Wasser. “segeln” here is the verb, to sail — not a form of the noun Segel, which stands next to it in the same sentence. “schifften … hin” is hinschiffen, to sail off in that direction; “Äcker” are ploughed fields, the driest ground there is.

sentences.t: da segelten sie über einen hohen Berg, da mußten sie elendig ersaufen.
sentences.l: there they sailed over a high mountain, there they had to drown miserably.
sentences.i: then they sailed over a high mountain, and there they had to drown wretchedly.
sentences.n: “elendig” is an older form of elend, ‘wretched, wretchedly.’ “ersaufen” is a coarse word for drowning, used of animals. Drowning on a mountain top is the point, and the tale reports it in the same flat voice as everything else.

sentences.t: Ein Krebs jagte einen Hasen in die Flucht,
sentences.l: A crab drove a hare into flight,
sentences.i: A crab put a hare to flight,
sentences.n: “in die Flucht jagen” = to put to flight. “Krebs” here is simply the crab or crayfish, the slowest hunter imaginable.

sentences.t: und hoch auf dem Dach lag eine Kuh, die war hinauf gestiegen.
sentences.l: and high on the roof lay a cow, she had climbed up.
sentences.i: and high on the roof lay a cow that had climbed up there.
sentences.n: “die war hinauf gestiegen” is hinaufsteigen split apart, with “hinauf” marking motion up and away from the speaker.

sentences.t: In dem Lande sind die Fliegen so groß als hier die Ziegen.
sentences.l: In that land the flies are as big as here the goats.
sentences.i: In that country the flies are as big as the goats are here.
sentences.n: “so groß als” is the older comparison where modern German has so groß wie. The teller slips into the present tense, as though reporting a plain fact about a place he knows.

sentences.t: Mache das Fenster auf, damit die Lügen hinaus fliegen.
sentences.l: Open the window, so that the lies fly out.
sentences.i: Open the window, so the lies can fly out.
sentences.n: “Mache … auf” is aufmachen, to open, split around its object. The last line hands the whole tale back to the listener as something to be got rid of, and stops there.

glossary.fein: fein — nicely; before an adverb, ‘nice and …’ (also fine, delicate)
glossary.gekehrt: kehren — turned (past part.; „gen Himmel gekehrt“ = turned toward heaven)
glossary.lahme: lahm — the lame man (adj. used as a noun: der Lahme). High German, not a dialect form
glossary.lahmen: lahm — the lame man (dat. sg. dem Lahmen, adj. used as a noun)
glossary.rühren: rühren — to stir, move (infinitive; „keinen Fuß rühren“ = not stir a foot)
glossary.segeln: segeln — to sail (infinitive); also die Segel ‘sails’ elsewhere
glossary.so: so — so, thus; „so groß als“ = as big as (older comparison, modern so groß wie)
glossary.spannten: spannen — spread, stretched (3rd pl. past; „die Segel spannen“ = to set the sails)
